subject: security
title: Systems Security
summary: Memory-safety bugs and layered defences: what each mitigation can protect, its requirements and its limits.

lessons.title: Buffers, boundaries and off-by-one errors
lessons.summary: A C buffer has an object boundary even when adjacent bytes are mapped and writable.
lessons.body:
C and C++ provide pointer operations without universal run-time bounds or lifetime checks. Accessing an object outside its bounds or lifetime can cause **undefined behaviour**: the language does not promise a clean crash, a particular overwrite, or access to arbitrary addresses. Operating-system mappings and permissions still constrain hardware accesses. The C examples below use the C11/C17 model. Memory-safe languages add those bounds and lifetime checks for you; a later lesson in this module covers what that changes and what it leaves.

These bugs can expose secrets or alter decisions as well as crash programs. Chromium reports that memory unsafety accounted for around 70% of a sample of 912 high/critical Stable-channel security bugs since 2015. This is a historical, project-specific sample, not a current universal percentage.

## Why a bug becomes a vulnerability

The diagram is an illustrative conventional process layout, not a C requirement (addresses increase upwards). Real systems may use multiple heap mappings; stack direction, saved registers and return-address storage depend on the architecture and compiler.

```
high  +------------------------+
      | stack (grows down)     |
      |  locals, saved regs,   |
      |  return addresses      |
      +------------------------+
      |         ...            |
      +------------------------+
      | heap (grows up)        |
      |  malloc'd objects and  |
      |  allocator metadata    |
      +------------------------+
      | globals, .data, .bss   |
      | program code (.text)   |
low   +------------------------+
```

The security concern is proximity: a buffer can share an allocation or stack frame with sensitive data. Depending on the implementation, nearby data can include control pointers or allocator metadata. Corrupting an authorisation flag can also compromise a program without hijacking control flow.

So a bug that writes past the end of a buffer does not just corrupt "some data". It can overwrite something that decides **what the program does next**. That is the step from crash to compromise, and it is why the defences later in this module focus on protecting that control data.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a paper form with fixed boxes
> A form has a box of 16 squares for your name, and right next to it a small box marked "Staff use: approved". Nothing about paper stops a pen at the edge of a box, so a very long name can run on into the approval box.
>
> **How it maps:** The boxes are neighbouring objects in a stack frame or allocation. The pen is `strcpy`, which keeps writing until the source ends, because it is never told where the box ends. Text spilling into "approved" is an overflow changing a nearby authorisation flag or control pointer.
>
> **Where it stops:** A C string also needs one square for its terminating NUL, so 16 bytes hold only 15 letters. On a form everyone can see which box comes next. In memory the compiler, ABI and allocator decide what is adjacent, and the C standard promises no particular result for the invalid write: it may corrupt data, crash or appear to work.

Two important families are spatial errors and temporal errors. This two-family split does not describe every issue below; uninitialised-value use also needs separate attention.

| Family | Question it breaks | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Spatial | Is this address inside the object? | Overflow, OOB read |
| Temporal | Is the object still alive? | Use-after-free, double free |

## Stack buffer overflow

The classic bug is copying input into a fixed-size buffer without checking its length.

```c
void greet(const char *name) {
    char buf[16];
    /* BUG: capacity is never checked. */
    strcpy(buf, name);
    /* Invalid copy: no promised output. */
    printf("Hello, %s\n", buf);
}
```

`strcpy` requires enough destination space for all source bytes and the terminating NUL, the zero byte that marks the end of a C string. It is never told the destination's size, so it cannot check. A string therefore needs one byte more than its length: the longest name that fits in `buf[16]` is 15 characters, and a 40-character name needs 41 bytes, 25 more than `buf` holds.

Calling it with such a name violates that requirement; a neighbouring-data overwrite is one possible result, not a guaranteed execution trace. A common review mistake is a length check that accepts names of up to 16 characters: it forgets the NUL, so a 16-character name still writes one byte too many. Include `<string.h>` and `<stdio.h>` when compiling these function fragments.

### Off-by-one errors

Many overflows are a single element too far:

```c
char id[8];
/* BUG: index eight is out of bounds. */
for (int i = 0; i <= 8; i++)
    id[i] = src[i];
```

With a source of at least nine bytes, the faulty loop attempts indices 0 through 8: nine writes into an eight-element array, whose valid indices are 0 through 7. For an eight-byte raw copy, use `i < 8` and a source of at least eight bytes. That correction does not create a NUL-terminated string: reserve and write a terminator if string APIs will consume the result.

## Key takeaways
- A C buffer has an object boundary even when adjacent bytes are mapped and writable.
- Copying a string requires space for its terminating NUL.
- An eight-element array has valid indices zero through seven; a raw copy does not create a string.

## Further reading
- [C11 committee draft: objects and library contracts](https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg14/www/docs/n1570.pdf)
- [Memory safety — Chromium](https://www.chromium.org/Home/chromium-security/memory-safety/)

options.text: Yes: every accepted name has at most 16 characters, and `buf` holds 16 bytes
options.explanation: This forgets the terminating NUL. `strcpy` copies the characters *and* the zero byte that ends the string, so a 16-character name needs 17 bytes.

options.text: No: a 16-character name needs 17 bytes including its NUL, so the check must also reject length 16
options.explanation: Correct. `strlen` does not count the NUL, but `strcpy` writes it. The longest name that fits is 15 characters, so the condition should reject any length of 16 or more (`>= sizeof buf`).

options.text: No: `strcpy` also appends a newline, so the limit must be 14 characters
options.explanation: `strcpy` copies the source bytes and one NUL; it adds no newline. The off-by-one is only the forgotten NUL.

options.text: Yes: `strcpy` stops at the end of `buf` anyway, so the check only saves time
options.explanation: `strcpy` is never told the destination size, so it cannot stop at the end of `buf`. That missing capacity argument is the root of the bug.

questions.workedExample:
1. `strlen(name)` counts the characters before the terminating NUL.
2. `strcpy` writes those characters and then the NUL, so it needs one byte more than `strlen` reports.
3. The check accepts a 16-character name. That copy needs 17 bytes, one more than `buf[16]` holds, so the call is invalid and its behaviour is undefined: it might corrupt a neighbouring byte, abort under a hardening check, or appear to work.
4. Fix the condition to reject `strlen(name) >= sizeof buf`, or better, use a bounded call such as `snprintf` and treat truncation as an error. Either way, the longest accepted name is 15 characters.

options.explanation: Classic off-by-one: this visits indices zero through eight, nine loop passes, and writes `id[8]`, which is one past the end.
Correct. Valid indices for an 8-element array are 0 to 7; `i < 8` stops after writing index 7.

options.text: `i <= sizeof id`
options.explanation: `sizeof id` is 8, so this is the same off-by-one as `i <= 8`.
Equivalent to `i <= 8`: nine loop passes, the last writing out of bounds.

questions.workedExample: For an eight-byte raw copy with at least eight readable source bytes, `i < 8` visits indices 0 through 7. Conditions allowing index 8 overrun the destination. This raw copy does not guarantee a NUL terminator; a string needs room for one and an explicit termination policy.

lessons.title: Bounded strings and explicit truncation
lessons.summary: Check snprintf for a negative error before interpreting its non-negative required length.

options.text: `11 [hello world]`
options.explanation: `snprintf` never writes more than `sizeof d` bytes, so the full string cannot be stored in an 8-byte buffer.

options.text: `7 [hello w]`
options.explanation: The contents are right but the return value is not the number of characters written; it is the length the full output *would* have had.

options.text: `11 [hello w]`
options.explanation: Correct. It stores 7 characters plus a NUL in the 8 bytes, and returns 11, the untruncated length. `n >= sizeof d` tells you it truncated.

options.text: `-1 [hello w]`
options.explanation: A negative return means a character encoding error, not truncation. C99 `snprintf` returns the would-be length on truncation.

questions.prompt: A reviewer replaces `strcpy(dst, src)` with `strncpy(dst, src, sizeof dst)` where `dst` is `char dst[4]` and the source string is `"abcdef"`. What is the remaining problem?

options.text: None; `strncpy` is the safe version of `strcpy`
options.explanation: This is the common misconception. `strncpy` bounds the write but does not guarantee a terminator.

options.text: `strncpy` still writes 7 bytes
options.explanation: It writes at most `n` = 4 bytes, so there is no write overflow here.

options.text: `dst` has no NUL terminator, so unbounded string operations on it are invalid
options.explanation: The four bytes are `abcd`, with no terminator. Passing that array to an unbounded string operation violates its input requirements and can over-read.

options.text: `strncpy` pads with spaces, corrupting the string
options.explanation: It fills the rest with NUL bytes, and only when the source is *shorter* than `n`.

questions.workedExample: Four source bytes fill `dst` as `abcd`; no NUL fits. An unbounded string operation is invalid on this result. Use a bounded formatting/copy API with error and truncation checks, or explicitly terminate within the destination while treating lost data as truncation. `strlcpy` is an option only where provided.

lessons.title: Validate the bytes that actually arrived
lessons.summary: A read past a live buffer is a spatial error and can disclose information.
lessons.body:
## Out-of-bounds reads: Heartbleed

Reading beyond an object can disclose memory if the result becomes observable. It may instead fault or have other undefined behaviour. Potential disclosures include secrets and addresses that weaken ASLR.

**Heartbleed** (CVE-2014-0160) in OpenSSL is the famous case. The TLS heartbeat message said "here are N bytes, echo them back". OpenSSL trusted the attacker-supplied N without checking it against how much data had actually arrived. Simplified:

```c
/* BUG: len is an untrusted claim. */
memcpy(reply, payload, len);  /* BUG */
```

A malformed request could make vulnerable OpenSSL disclose up to 64 KB of process memory, potentially including secrets. A crash or other outcome was also possible. The 64 KB limit comes from the length field: it is two bytes (16 bits), so the largest length it can claim is 65,535 bytes, just under 64 KiB. That cap applies to each heartbeat, not to the attack: an attacker could keep sending requests and collect more chunks of memory.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: reading back a message by its claimed length
> A caller hands a receptionist a note and says "please read my 500-word message back to me". The note holds five words, but the receptionist trusts the number and keeps reading aloud from whatever papers lie underneath: other visitors' messages, a door code, a phone number.
>
> **How it maps:** The note is the heartbeat payload, the spoken "500" is the attacker-supplied length field, and the papers underneath are neighbouring heap memory. The receptionist's mistake is the missing check: compare the claimed length with what actually arrived.
>
> **Where it stops:** Heap memory is not a tidy pile of documents. What lies beyond the payload depends on the allocator and timing, the read may fault instead, and the 16-bit length field caps each reply at about 64 KB.

A heartbeat message (RFC 6520) is laid out as a one-byte type, the two-byte payload length, the payload, then at least 16 bytes of random padding. Everything the length claims must fit inside what actually arrived:

```formula essential
1 + 2 + L + 16 ≤ R
L ≤ R − 19
where
1: the one-byte message type
2: the two-byte payload-length field
L: the payload length the message claims, in bytes; attacker-controlled (len in the code)
16: the minimum padding, in bytes, that RFC 6520 requires after the payload
19: the header and minimum padding together (1 + 2 + 16 bytes)
R: the number of bytes of heartbeat message actually received (record_len in the code)
≤: less than or equal to
In words: the header, the claimed payload and the minimum padding must all fit in the received bytes, so the claimed length can be at most the received size minus 19.
```

For example, if 40 bytes arrive, the payload can be at most 21 bytes, and a claimed length of 65,535 must be rejected. Vulnerable OpenSSL skipped this check and copied as many bytes as were claimed, reading far past the real payload.

So first ensure the three-byte header exists before parsing its length, and reserve the required minimum 16-byte padding too. `size_t` is unsigned, so if `record_len` were below 19, `record_len - 3 - 16` would wrap to a huge number (integer wraparound) and the length check would pass. With non-negative `size_t` lengths and a sufficiently large reply buffer, the following guard prevents that subtraction underflow:

```c
/* Guard subtraction before checking len. */
if (record_len < 3 + 16)
    return 0;
if (len > record_len - 3 - 16)
    return 0;  /* discard bad message */
/* Both ranges must fit and not overlap. */
memcpy(reply, payload, len);
```

Treat externally supplied lengths, indices and counts as untrusted. Validate both the arithmetic and the resulting range against actual available storage before parsing or copying.

## Key takeaways
- A read past a live buffer is a spatial error and can disclose information.
- Validate the heartbeat header before parsing its claimed length, then account for minimum padding.
- Guard unsigned subtraction before using a received length to derive a remaining capacity.

## Further reading
- [Heartbleed advisory — OpenSSL](https://openssl-library.org/news/secadv/20140407.txt)
- [TLS heartbeat — RFC 6520](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6520.html)
- [The Heartbleed Bug](https://heartbleed.com/)

questions.prompt: A malformed Heartbleed request supplied fewer payload bytes than its length field claimed. Which behaviour made the vulnerable OpenSSL implementation an information-disclosure vulnerability?

options.text: Crashed immediately on the oversized length
options.explanation: A crash was possible, but was not a reliable protection. The vulnerability could disclose process memory rather than rejecting every malformed request.

options.text: It could copy beyond the supplied payload into a response, disclosing up to about 64 KB
options.explanation: Correct. `memcpy` used the attacker's length without checking it against the record's real size, so it over-read adjacent heap memory, which could hold keys and cookies.

options.text: Wrote 64 KB of attacker data over its heap
options.explanation: Heartbleed was an out-of-bounds *read* (an information leak), not a write.

options.text: Rejected the message because TLS records are authenticated
options.explanation: The heartbeat was processed inside the TLS layer; record authentication does not validate this inner length field.

questions.workedExample:
1. A heartbeat request contains a one-byte type, a two-byte payload length, the payload and at least 16 bytes of random padding.
2. The vulnerable code used the claimed length in `memcpy` without comparing it with the bytes that had actually arrived.
3. When the claim was larger than the real payload, the copy read past it into neighbouring heap memory and sent those bytes back in the response. That is an out-of-bounds *read*: it discloses data rather than overwriting it.
4. A two-byte field can claim up to 65,535 bytes, which is where the roughly 64 KB per-request limit comes from.
5. A robust parser checks that the header is present, then that the claimed payload plus the 19 bytes of header and minimum padding fit in what arrived. With 40 bytes received, any claim above 21 is discarded.

The review does not assume every malformed maximum-length request yields an identical complete reply.

lessons.title: Check arithmetic before allocating
lessons.summary: Unsigned wraparound is defined arithmetic, but a wrapped allocation size can lead to invalid accesses.
lessons.body:
## Integer overflow leading to a small allocation

Size arithmetic can suffer integer wraparound. Consider:

```c
/* BUG: product may wrap before malloc. */
/* count comes from a file header. */
item *arr = malloc(count * sizeof(item));
/* No allocation-failure check here. */
for (uint32_t i = 0; i < count; i++)
    read_item(&arr[i]);
```

Assume both `count` and `size_t` are 32-bit unsigned types, and `sizeof(item)` is 16. C's unsigned arithmetic does not fail when a result is too big: it keeps only the lowest 32 bits of the result and silently drops the rest (this is called modular arithmetic). With a hostile header the numbers look like this:

```c
/* 32-bit size_t, sizeof(item) == 16   */
/* count       = 0x10000001            */
/* true bytes  = 0x100000010 (33 bits) */
/* malloc gets = 0x00000010 = 16 bytes */
```

About 268 million items should need about 4 GiB, but the 33rd bit is dropped and `malloc` is asked for just 16 bytes. Allocation may fail; if it succeeds, the loop's item writes run far past that 16-byte allocation, a heap overflow with undefined behaviour.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a car odometer rolling over
> A five-digit mileage counter that reads 99,990 shows 00,006 after another 16 miles. Nothing breaks and no warning appears: the counter simply has no digit for the carry.
>
> **How it maps:** The counter's digits are the 32 bits of `size_t`. The lost carry is the 33rd bit of `count * sizeof(item)`. A buyer trusting the low reading is `malloc` trusting the small wrapped size.
>
> **Where it stops:** An odometer counts in decimal and its rollover is obvious to a person; unsigned C arithmetic is binary, and nothing in the program notices unless the code checks before multiplying.

The standard check avoids the multiplication altogether. The product fits only if it is no larger than `SIZE_MAX`, the largest value `size_t` can hold. Dividing `SIZE_MAX` by the item size gives the largest safe count, and that division cannot itself overflow. With a 32-bit `size_t` and 16-byte items the largest safe count is 268,435,455, so the count 268,435,457 (`0x10000001`) above is rejected.

Fixes:

- Check before multiplying: `if (count > SIZE_MAX / sizeof(item)) fail;`
- On documented implementations such as glibc, `calloc(count, sizeof(item))` and `reallocarray` reject size overflow. `reallocarray` is POSIX, not ISO C. Check allocation failure before dereferencing; define a policy for zero counts.
- Reject absurd values early: a sane maximum for `count` is good input validation anyway.

## Key takeaways
- Unsigned wraparound is defined arithmetic, but a wrapped allocation size can lead to invalid accesses.
- Check the count against SIZE_MAX divided by the item size before multiplying.
- Apply application-specific count limits and handle allocation failure and zero-count policy even when overflow is rejected.

## Further reading
- [C11 committee draft: objects and library contracts](https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg14/www/docs/n1570.pdf)
- [Allocating cleared space — glibc](https://sourceware.org/glibc/manual/latest/html_node/Allocating-Cleared-Space.html)
- [reallocarray — POSIX](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9799919799/functions/reallocarray.html)

options.text: The product wrapped to a 16-byte request; reject `count > SIZE_MAX / sizeof(item)` (and apply a sane limit) before allocating
options.explanation: Correct. 0x10000001 × 16 is 0x100000010, which needs 33 bits; keeping the low 32 bits leaves 0x10, so `malloc` returned a 16-byte block that the loop overran. Checking the count against `SIZE_MAX / sizeof(item)` before multiplying, or using `calloc`/`reallocarray`, which reject the overflow on glibc, removes the cause.

options.text: An off-by-one in the loop; stop it one item earlier
options.explanation: The loop visits indices from 0 up to one less than `count`, which matches the intended array. The allocation is what is too small: stopping one item earlier would still write about 268 million items into 16 bytes.

options.text: Signed overflow is undefined; build with `-fwrapv`
options.explanation: Both operands are unsigned, and C already defines unsigned wraparound. `-fwrapv` defines *signed* wrapping and would not make the 16-byte allocation large enough.

options.text: `malloc` returned a fragmented block; check for `NULL` and retry
options.explanation: A `NULL` check is still required, but here `malloc` succeeded and returned exactly the 16 bytes it was asked for. Retrying asks for the same wrong size.

questions.workedExample:
1. The fuzzer's crash is a write past the allocation, so ask why the allocation is smaller than the loop expects.
2. The intended size is about 268 million items of 16 bytes, around 4 GiB. That needs 33 bits, but a 32-bit `size_t` keeps only the lowest 32: 0x100000010 becomes 0x10, a 16-byte request.
3. Unsigned wraparound is defined C behaviour, so nothing traps; `malloc` succeeds and the loop writes far beyond it.
4. The fix belongs before the multiplication: reject `count > SIZE_MAX / sizeof(item)`, apply an application limit on `count`, and still handle allocation failure. On implementations such as glibc, `calloc(count, sizeof(item))` and `reallocarray` perform the overflow check for you, but their return values must still be checked.

lessons.title: Lifetimes, stale aliases and ownership
lessons.summary: Freeing an allocation ends its lifetime; an address remaining mapped does not keep the object alive.
lessons.body:
## Use-after-free

A **use-after-free** (UAF) is a temporal bug: the program keeps using a pointer after the memory it points to has been released.

```c
struct session *s = load_session();
/* The owning pointer is not cleared. */
if (expired(s))
    free(s);
/* ... later, on another path ... */
/* BUG: the old object may be gone. */
if (s->is_admin)
    grant_access();
```

An allocator may reuse freed storage for a later allocation. If request-controlled bytes occupy that storage, a dangling access can influence an authorisation decision or a control pointer. Reuse timing is allocator-dependent, and undefined behaviour means no particular result is guaranteed. The fragment assumes `load_session` succeeded; real code must also handle failure.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a hotel key that still opens the old room
> You check out of a hotel but keep your key card. If the hotel forgot to re-code the lock, the card still opens room 412, which now holds the next guest's luggage.
>
> **How it maps:** The room is a block of heap storage, checking out is `free`, the next guest is a new allocation that reuses the storage, and the kept key card is a dangling pointer. Reading `s->is_admin` is opening the door and trusting whatever is now inside.
>
> **Where it stops:** A hotel can re-code every lock at checkout; C's `free` does nothing to the pointers you still hold, and nothing announces that the room has a new occupant. Whether and when storage is reused is up to the allocator, and the invalid access has undefined behaviour rather than a predictable result.

Defences in C:

- After `free`, setting an owning pointer to `NULL` can support later explicit null checks and makes `free(NULL)` harmless. Dereferencing NULL is still undefined behaviour, not a guaranteed clean crash; other aliases still dangle.
- Give every allocation **one clear owner** responsible for freeing it, and document which functions borrow versus take ownership.
- In C++, prefer `std::unique_ptr` when one owner holds the object, using `std::shared_ptr` when ownership really is shared. Raw borrowed aliases and unsynchronised access still require lifetime discipline.

An AddressSanitizer test build can catch many accesses while released storage remains poisoned. An access after that address has been reused for a live allocation may escape this check; the underlying lifetime error still needs repair.

### Double free

Freeing the same allocation twice is undefined behaviour; `free(NULL)` is exempt. Outcomes can include allocator corruption or a diagnostic abort. Whether a double free is detected is implementation-dependent, and detecting it does not make double free safe. Clear ownership and avoiding stale aliases prevent the underlying error.

## What a memory-safe language changes

C and C++ leave both questions, "is this index inside the object?" and "is this object still alive?", to the programmer. A **memory-safe language** answers them in the language itself:

- **Bounds are checked.** In Java, an array index below zero or at least the array's length throws `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`. In Rust, indexing a vector past its end causes a Rust panic, and `v.get(i)` returns `None` for the code to handle. Either way the neighbouring bytes are never read or written.
- **Lifetimes are enforced.** Java programs never free objects explicitly: a garbage collector reclaims only objects that nothing can still reach, so a reference that still exists keeps its object alive instead of pointing into reused storage. Safe Rust has no garbage collector: its ownership rules and **borrow checker** reject, at compile time, code that uses a value after it has been moved or dropped, keeps a reference longer than the value lives, or would free it twice.

So spatial and temporal bugs no longer corrupt memory without warning. They become a compile-time error or a defined, contained failure. That is why, in December 2023, CISA, NSA, the FBI and partner agencies in Australia, Canada, the UK and New Zealand urged software makers to publish **memory-safe roadmaps** for moving to memory-safe languages, and why CISA and NSA repeated the case in joint guidance in June 2025.

What it does not remove:

- **Unchecked code.** In unsafe Rust (code inside an `unsafe` block), the programmer can dereference raw pointers and call C functions through a foreign function interface (FFI); the compiler does not check those operations for memory safety. Bugs in linked C or C++ libraries remain.
- **Crashes.** A panic or exception is still an availability failure if nothing handles it.
- **Other bug classes.** Logic and authorisation errors remain. Ported to Java, the session example above would no longer read reused memory: the stale reference keeps the old, expired session alive, and the code could still grant access to it. The missing "is this session still valid?" check is a logic bug. The 2023 roadmap guidance itself notes that memory-safe languages are not free from other critical vulnerabilities.

## Key takeaways
- Freeing an allocation ends its lifetime; an address remaining mapped does not keep the object alive.
- Nulling one owning pointer does not repair other aliases.
- Clear ownership and disciplined borrowing address the cause of use-after-free and double free.
- Memory-safe languages turn bounds and lifetime errors into compile errors or defined failures; `unsafe` code, foreign libraries and logic bugs remain.

## Further reading
- [AddressSanitizer — Clang](https://clang.llvm.org/docs/AddressSanitizer.html)
- [C11 committee draft: objects and library contracts](https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg14/www/docs/n1570.pdf)
- [CWE-416: use after free — MITRE](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/416.html)
- [The Case for Memory Safe Roadmaps — CISA and partners](https://www.cisa.gov/resources-tools/resources/case-memory-safe-roadmaps)
- [What is ownership? — The Rust Programming Language](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch04-01-what-is-ownership.html)

questions.prompt: A team rewrites a C session handler in safe Rust, with no `unsafe` blocks and no C libraries. Which problem from the C version can **still** occur?

options.text: Reading `s->name` after the session was freed and its storage reused
options.explanation: That is a temporal (lifetime) error. Safe Rust's ownership rules and borrow checker reject use of a value after it has been moved or dropped at compile time, so this C use-after-free cannot be written in safe code.

options.text: Writing index 16 of a 16-element buffer and silently changing the next variable
options.explanation: That is a spatial (bounds) error. Rust checks indexing: an out-of-range index causes a panic instead of touching neighbouring bytes. The program may still stop, but it does not silently corrupt memory.

options.text: Granting admin access to a session whose expiry the code never checks
options.explanation: Correct. This is a logic and authorisation bug, not a memory-safety bug. A memory-safe language guarantees that `is_admin` is read from a live, valid object; it cannot know that the object should no longer be trusted.

options.text: Freeing the same session twice and corrupting the allocator
options.explanation: Double free is a temporal error. Each Rust value has one owner that drops it once, and the compiler rejects code that would use or drop a moved value, so safe code cannot free it twice.

questions.workedExample:
1. Sort the options into memory-safety classes. Writing past a buffer is **spatial** (is the address inside the object?). Use-after-free and double free are **temporal** (is the object still alive?).
2. Safe Rust removes both classes: indexing is bounds-checked at run time (a panic instead of corruption), and ownership with the borrow checker rejects use-after-move and double drop at compile time.
3. What remains is behaviour the program was *allowed* to do: reading a valid session's `is_admin` field and acting on it. If the code never checks expiry, that authorisation flaw survives any language change.
4. `unsafe` code and foreign C libraries are excluded by the prompt; with them, memory bugs could return in that code.
